title: Dogen's Refrain From Evil Part 1
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: Zoketsu Norman Fischer takes up Dogen's fascicle "Refrain from Unwholesome Action" on Juneteenth, reading selected passages on the three pure precepts: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind. Norman explains that the seven original Buddhas stand for infinite Buddhas, so the precepts have no first moment, and that transmitting, receiving, and practicing them is one shared activity. Examples of changing customs, from radio profanity to summer clothing, show how good and bad shift with conditions. Anger in the name of compassion becomes its own unwholesome action, and bodhisattvas turn anger into energy as wrathful protectors of the Dharma. Norman closes with Dogen's claim that refraining from evil is actualized across the whole universe, and with a physicist's book about time that a brother sent.

I'm trying not to move my head around so much.
But if you find that it's hard to hear, just wave your hand in the back.
I'm not sure what happened.
Maybe my voice got low.
Sorry.
So please let me know tomorrow.
Let me know tomorrow, today.
Yes.
Okay.
I've got all my stuff here.
Did I push this button?
I pushed all the buttons.
I turned everything on.
Okay.
Well, first of all, I want to wish you all a happy Juneteenth.
Today is Juneteenth, a great and underappreciated American holiday, which marks the day, June 19th, 1865.
It was not actually a major occurrence, like a battle wasn't won or anything like that.

But on that day, General Gordon Granger marched his Union soldiers into Galveston, Texas, to let people there know what had happened a while before that: that the Emancipation Proclamation had been signed and that there were no more slaves in the United States.
People didn't know that until he told them on June 19th.
So it's a very, very happy day, a day for liberation and celebration of the fact that despite everything, sometimes even at great cost, people do do the right thing.
So, happy Juneteenth.
This morning I'm going to give probably a complicated talk, and I apologize in advance if it turns out to be too complicated.
I'm going to try my best to make myself understood, but as I always say, even if not, and even if you can't hear my words in the back, it doesn't matter that much, really.
It's worthwhile anyway, just to sit here and fulfill the ritual of Dharma talk.
The actual Dharma is subtle and profound and very hard to understand, probably realistically impossible to understand.
And I will be the first to tell you that I myself definitely don't understand it.
Not only that, but I don't even know the languages in which the teachings are written down.
I can't read any of those languages.
I'm like a total idiot when it comes to understanding the Dharma.
So really, I'm like a baby baffled by a bewildering world and sort of wanting, like a baby does, to understand, but not yet ready to understand.
I freely admit that in the beginning, partly to let myself off the hook, but also partly because it's honest and it's real.
But clearly there is a virtue in making the effort to understand.
That's the only way we'll ever understand it, if we make the effort.
And this is what we human beings always do.
We make the effort to understand.
It's very important, really, that we make this effort, however unsuccessful we may be at it.
If we only succeed in letting ourselves know that we don't understand, I think that's a lot already.

That's important, because if we keep going on in this way that we're going on here, thinking that we do know who we are, we do know what's going on all around us, we will just go on continuing to make a big mess in our own lives and in the world.
So a little bit of bafflement and not understanding is very good for us, and it goes a long way.

Anyway, the reason I'm bringing this up today, on Juneteenth, this very difficult fascicle of Dogen called Refrain from Unwholesome Action, Shohaku Makusa, is that I know many of us are pretty baffled by and upset about the world we're living in in our time.
It's upsetting, as it ought to be, because we all want the world to be good.
We want the world to be just and moral.
We want a world in which evil action, unwholesome action, does not rule the day, a world in which good action, wholesome action, is the way the world is.
And that's what Dogen is writing about in this fascicle.
So I thought it would be worth reading it together, even if we don't completely understand it, because it's actually a difficult, lengthy piece of writing, but we're going to try it.
What does it really mean for us to live a life according to goodness?
What does it mean in the world, for the world to be a good world, for goodness to rule the world?
Like I say, it's a pretty long fascicle.
I'm not going to try to read through all of it.
I'm just picking out parts that I think touch the main points.
So let's see what happens.
Here are the opening lines.
*Ancient Buddhas say, refrain from unwholesome action.
Do wholesome action.
Purify your own mind.*
*This is the teaching of all Buddhas.
This teaching has been authentically transmitted from earlier Buddhas to later Buddhas and to Buddhas of the future as the seven original Buddhas, general precepts in the ancestral school.
Later Buddhas received these precepts from earlier Buddhas.
And this teaching is not limited to the seven original Buddhas.
It is the teaching of all Buddhas.
So, thoroughly investigate this point.
This Dharma way of the seven original Buddhas is always the Dharma way of the seven original Buddhas.
Transmitting and receiving these precepts is a mutual activity.
This is the teaching of all Buddhas.
The teaching, practice, and enlightenment of hundreds, thousands, and myriads of Buddhas,* meaning an infinitude of Buddhas.
We all know about these three precepts.
We call them the three pure precepts.
Using the fewest words, they would be: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind.
They're very, very ancient in Buddhism, and they couldn't be more basic.
They seem pretty straightforward, but as we will learn, there's a lot more to them than there seems to be.
If you read almost any book about Buddhism, it will say that Prince Siddhartha, who later became Buddha, went forth from the home life.
He practiced austerities and hard practice of all kinds.
He became awakened and then went forth to start what we now call Buddhism.
He was the first Buddha.
But in Zen practice, the understanding is that nothing begins, nothing ends, and nothing begins.
This echoes back to Tim's talk the other day about time.
The teachings about time, when you delve into them, always seem so abstract.
Even though they're engaging, they seem abstract, but they're not really abstract.
If we view our lives as something that begins at a point in time and goes along in time in a linear fashion, and then is gone, we're missing our life, as Dogen teaches.
The depth of our life comes from the way we understand our life and hold our life.
And the way we hold our life and bring ourselves to our life is different when we understand that we're not just living in a linear way.
We're living in an all-inclusive way.
There's more to what's happening than meets the eye.
Everything is here on your cushion.
It's not just you and your little problems sitting there.
This is literally actually true.
Everything is going on right there where you are all the time.
When you know this about your life, when you feel this about your life to the core, as the fruit of many decades of practice, you are then living a very different life.
The same?
Nobody notices, maybe, but very different.
That's what's implied here when Dogen is telling us that no, it's not what it says in the book.
The Buddha was not the first Buddha.
There were seven Buddhas before Buddha.
Those seven Buddhas are mythical Buddhas that stand for infinite Buddhas before Buddha.
No one invented the three pure precepts.
They have always existed.
They always will exist.
This is the basic way of practice throughout space and time.
It never started, it never ends.
When Dogen says, as he so often does, investigate this, he's telling us that his words are merely indicating something that we need to see for ourselves.
There's a lot more here that we need to investigate for ourselves.
I sometimes wonder whether, when Dogen was giving fascicles of the Shobogenzo, like this one, as talks to the monastic assembly, I wonder whether when he said, investigate this...
It's louder when I turn my head this way, right?
Is that right?

I wonder whether when he said, investigate this, he actually stopped talking and sat there with everybody for five or ten or twenty or sixty or seventy or ninety minutes, while everybody investigated this.
So yes, investigate this.
Investigate these very simple ABC teachings of the three pure precepts and see if you can find more in them than you thought was there.
In the rest of the fascicle, he's going to try to indicate what else might be there.
He also says, in the passage I read, that transmitting and receiving these precepts is a mutual activity.
We think of the practice of precepts as my practice, me deciding what is right and wrong to do, me and my choices that I will feel good about or not good about.
But here he's saying, no, there's more to it than that, because precepts are not just practiced, they are transmitted and received.
In Zen, this all is one activity.
Transmitting, receiving, practicing is all one activity.
This is what we do in all our Zen rituals.
We're always transmitting, receiving, and practicing precepts in every one of our rituals, because this is our main practice.
Actually, it's identical to the practice of zazen, although it takes some decades to see this point, because we think zazen is meditation.
But actually, it's not.

It's receiving, transmitting, and practicing precepts, which Dogen says here is a mutual activity handed down from the endless Buddhas to the endless Buddhas right here and now at this moment of your life on your cushion.
It's a shared life together.
It's a shared heart.
And probably, I think, that's the secret of what Dogen is wanting to tell us.
Maybe that's why there is no first Buddha, there couldn't be a first Buddha.
Why there's no one minute and the next minute and the next minute and the next minute, why it couldn't be like that.
Because all the time, if only we could open to it, we would realize we're living a shared heart.
All the time, we are not in control.
We do not contain our lives or our actions.
All the time, we are receiving and transmitting precepts, and we think of it as my life.
So much more is life than my life.
He goes on.
*Unwholesome action, or evil or bad action, unwholesome action is a manifestation of one of the three natures.* The three natures are wholesome action, unwholesome action, and neutral action.
*The unwholesome action nature is unborn, unborn.
Just as the wholesome action nature and the neutral nature are unborn, these three natures are also undefiled, and they are reality.
However, these three natures are manifested in various ways.*
So he says there are three, this very traditional thing to say.
There are three kinds of actions: wholesome or good actions, unwholesome or bad actions, and neutral actions or mixed actions.
Wholesome actions lead to wholesome, positive, happy results.
Unwholesome actions lead to trouble, and neutral actions, we're not sure.
Sometimes this way, sometimes that way, or sometimes neutral.
And this is a lawful universe.
It works like that.
No exceptions.
So when we look at the world now, and we think it's a wreck, we can't bear it.
Naturally, we're looking for the culprit.
How did this happen?
I didn't do it.
What happened?
We look for mistakes.
We look for graspable causes.
We blame people.
Sometimes we blame ourselves, in the case of our own misfortunes.
We blame somebody, or we blame ourselves.
We blame ideas, or organizations, or human tendencies.
But persons and ideas and organizations can only gain power when the conditions that make that possible obtain.
And when those conditions obtain, many, many conditions beyond what we can ever understand, we will have what we have in the present moment.
So really, it's the sum total of human activity that produces this moment.
Or, if we take just our own locality, the sum total of the actions of Americans over many hundreds of years, from the time there were what we call Americans, has produced the present conditions.
Things as they are now, wherever we look, do not come from nowhere.
They do not come from mistakes or accidents.
They are as they are and as they must be.
So when we understand that actions have consequences and that actions mutually produce present moments, we are never surprised or dismayed by what happens.
Of course these things will happen, when we consider the sum total of what we have done to one another over all these millennia.
We understand, with great sorrow perhaps, but with a settled heart.

When Dogen says the three natures are manifested in different ways, he's pointing out something very obvious: something that's considered good in one time or place can be considered a bad thing in another time or place.
So, oddly, good, bad and neutral are firm and indelible aspects of reality.
There's no question about them.
And yet they will appear differently depending on conditions.
Later he says what's good and bad is different in the god realm or the hell realm or the Buddha realm.
We don't need god realms or Buddha realms to see that this is true.
For instance, not long ago it used to be forbidden to say certain words on the radio or on television.
These were indecent, shocking words, and now you read them in the New York Times and you hear them on every podcast.
Sometimes people in political podcasts start using profanity for no particular reason, just because it's colloquial speech now.

People used to be terribly ashamed of their suffering and their sad stories, but now they write a memoir and it becomes a bestseller about all the things that happened to them, and then they discuss them on the television and it's common.
It used to be you couldn't drink alcohol.
It was illegal.
Now it's advertised everywhere and it's pretty good.
Everybody likes to drink alcohol.
Where we live, when it gets really hot, you can put on a tank top and short shorts and flip flops.
Who wants to put on a lot of clothes?
When it's really hot it would be crazy.
But in other parts of the world, especially women, no way.
We don't care what the temperature is.
You keep your entire body covered.
So Dogen is just saying that there's good and bad and neutral, but whenever we say this or that particular thing is good or bad or neutral, we have to think again.
It all goes according to custom and the sensibilities of people in a place at a particular time.
I think we all know that, but sometimes we forget it and we get pretty agitated about what we think is good or bad.
Then Dogen says these three natures are unborn and undefiled.
That's a little jarring.
What does he mean?
They're unborn and undefiled.
He means there is nothing inherently good or bad in them.
They are empty.
They are perfect.
Both unwholesome and wholesome action are undefiled and unborn.
So we can see this is wholesome and this is unwholesome, and we can know what to do or not do.
That's pretty clear.
But there's nothing fundamentally, truly, really good or bad about any action.
In all action, everything that happens is just, as he's saying, reality.
It is.
And there is always something very important about what is.
You have to respect what is, even when you don't like it.
A lot of times we're actually denying what is.
This isn't so when it is so.
You have to respect what is the case, even when you don't like it.
And we can really wreck our lives and make ourselves crazy because what is is not what we want it to be.
Of course, we follow the precepts.
We avoid evil.
We do good.
But whatever is the case is unborn and undefiled.
It is floating.
It is free of its marks and characteristics.
And there is always something awesome and sacred and timeless about what actually is the case.
That's what we need to discover.

So Dogen is telling us that if we really want to practice, refrain from evil and do good, we should understand this about the nature of doing evil and good and not get caught up in our wants and desires and preferences.
Of course, we're going to have our wants and desires and preferences.
Of course, we are all going to be conditioned by what has happened to us, by our upbringing, by our education and associations.
We can't not be that person.
Maybe even we could admit to ourselves that we're a little selfish and self-centered.
But honestly, I'm pretty sure that everybody sitting here now listening to me, and probably most people, can see through themselves when they're selfish and can behave decently.
I think we all do that.
We're not outrageously selfish individuals.
We're trying to be good.
And I think most people are.
But we get caught.
We get caught in our notions of right and wrong.
Then we ascribe, without knowing we're doing it, a kind of metaphysical or substantial reality to right and wrong, onto which we project our sense of self-respect.
And then we get upset.
We say, "That is wrong.
I can't bear it.
I can't allow it.
And it's not about me.
It's not about what I want.
It's about love.
It's about compassion.
And I hate those sons of bitches who are not loving and compassionate.
I'm really completely against them.
Because it's not about me.
It's about right and wrong.
It's not just my preference.
I am duty-bound to hate those uncompassionate people."
As if, if I didn't hate them and oppose them, I would lose myself.
So it's a desperate thing.
As if there actually were those people, as if they did exist in the way I think they do.
I'm so convinced they do.
And before you know it, based on this kind of confusion, we're all tied up in knots together, pulling tighter and tighter and squeezing one another.
Then it's really hard to avoid evil and do good and purify the mind.
And then we're in a big battle, partly with ourselves, partly with others we imagine to be this way or that way.
And they never are, of course, according to our ideas of right and wrong and our projections of a substantial world with non-empty individuals in it.
So this is a very astonishing thing.
We've been doing this forever.
Dogen is trying to straighten this out.
He's saying, yes, it is absolutely basic and crucial.
All Buddhas have always taught it from the beginning of time: avoid evil, do good, purify the mind.
And there is actually no good or evil.
There is only what is.
There is only reality.
There is only what ineffably occurs in front of us that we do not understand and never will.
Maybe it's obvious to you that being angry and hateful, in the name of compassion and peacefulness, is itself not avoiding evil.
As we know from our precept study, to harbor anger is unwholesome.
So getting angry and upset about bad actions on the part of other people is not exactly practicing the precepts.
It's itself bad action.
But maybe we say, "Well, anger is also a good thing.
If my anger gets me up off my butt and causes me to address injustice, isn't that a good thing?"
And that's true, too.
In the teachings it says bodhisattvas sometimes break precepts out of love for sentient beings.
And this fascicle, Dogen, says that.
He says non-bodhisattva practitioners always have to follow the precepts to the letter, but bodhisattva practitioners sometimes break precepts out of love for sentient beings.
But even then, even when our anger stirs us up to action, if we're harboring anger, and if we see someone evil to be angry with, things won't go well.
That's not how bodhisattvas practice.
Bodhisattvas see through their anger and transmute it into energy and strength.
They become wrathful deities protecting the Dharma, not self-righteous people whacking other people over the head with their self-righteous identities.
Which takes some practice.
It takes a while.
It takes having to be uncomfortable sometimes.
It takes having to think twice, three times, four times.
Then Dogen says, a little later:
*There's a great difference between the Buddha way and the worldly realm in what is called unwholesome action, wholesome action or neutral action.
Wholesome action and unwholesome action are time.*
What?
*Wholesome action and unwholesome action are time.
Although time is neither wholesome action nor unwholesome action.
Wholesome action and unwholesome action are Dharma.
Both of them are time.
Both of them are Dharma.
Although Dharma is neither wholesome action nor unwholesome action.
As Dharma is all inclusive, unwholesome action is all inclusive.
As Dharma is all inclusive, wholesome action is all inclusive.*
So these are some surprising and important points that Dogen is making in this passage.

I think most of us probably haven't necessarily thought about this much, but I think we assume that the morality of wholesome and unwholesome, good and bad, is the same in the worldly realm and also in the Buddha way.
There is a certain amount of overlap, so it makes sense we would look at it that way.
And you look around and Buddhists are, on the whole, more or less pretty well-behaved, polite people.
But at the level of Dharma that Dogen is now speaking about, there's a big difference between the worldly realm and the Buddha way.
In the worldly realm, unwholesome is bad, period.
Often it's even illegal, or if it's not, we'll pass a law.
We condemn bad behavior and bad people.
And it's pretty clear what's bad and what's good.
But astonishingly, Dogen here says that in the Buddha way, wholesome action and unwholesome action are Dharma and are time.
Both are reality.
Both are ineffably profound and subtle.
What is, is.
What is, is all of time and Dharma, including our enemies and their bad actions.
And all of this, he writes, wholesome and unwholesome alike, is all inclusive.
All this is so provocative, right?
What is he telling us?
The terrible things that happen in our personal lives.
The terrible things that happen in the world around us.
These things are sacred reality.
These things are all-inclusive time.
The tragedy of our lives, the tragedy of the historical moment in which we are living, is reverberating forever throughout the cosmos.
It is the cosmos.
So if we took this to heart, what in the world would this mean to us?
How would we live?
It means that when we would see this point, we would refrain from unwholesome action.
We would do good action.
And we would understand, as we did that, with our whole heart, that there is a poignancy to what happens far beyond our preferences and our way of seeing things.
We would understand that something immense is unfolding, not only in big events of our lives or big historical moments, but all the time, moment by moment by moment.
Those big events and big historical occasions are just markers for something that is immensely unfolding moment by moment by moment.
We will know what to do and what not to do.
It will be very, very clear to us.
And yet we will understand that we will never be able to completely see what is unfolding before our very eyes.
We will never know the consequences and the destiny that will flow forth from this moment.
When we get upset, we think, "I know what's going to happen.
I know what's going to happen.
That's why I'm so upset, because I know what's going to happen."
We never know what's going to happen.
We don't know.
So whenever we act, we will feel that point in our heart.
We will feel it in our very body, in our thinking.
And we will act, respecting this deep teaching.
He goes on:
*When you listen, study, practice, and realize unsurpassable, complete enlightenment, it is deep, vast, and wondrous.
You learn this unsurpassable enlightenment either by following a teacher or by following a sutra.
And the first thing you understand is refrain from unwholesome action.
If you don't understand refrain from unwholesome action, it can't be the true Buddha Dharma.
It must be the speech of demons.
Know that to understand unsurpassable enlightenment as refrain from unwholesome action is the true Buddha Dharma.
Refrain from unwholesome action.*
*This is not what ordinary people first interpret it to mean.
Although it may sound like it when we hear enlightenment expounded as a teaching of enlightenment, we understand in this way because it is an expression of unsurpassable enlightenment.
It is words of enlightenment.
Therefore, it is spoken enlightenment.
Moved by what is spoken and heard unsurpassable enlightenment, you vow to refrain from unwholesome action and practice refraining from unwholesome action.*
So here Dogen is making a further point.
He's extending what he's saying still further.
I hope I haven't confused you by using different words.
When I say avoid evil, do good, it's the same.
You understand that, right?
The same as refrain from unwholesome action and do good action.
Just another translation of the same words.
The reason I mention that at this point is because now Dogen is talking about words.
The words "refrain from unwholesome action."
Dogen really understands, perhaps as no other Buddhist teacher in history did, the almost mystical and double-edged power of words to create the world we live in with all of its beauty and suffering.
Just like in the Bible, "let there be light."
Somebody says, it happens to be God, but still, somebody says, "let there be light," and kaboom, there's light.
Have you ever noticed that?
There's no machinery, there's no materials.
The words are spoken, and it's so.
Words create worlds.
Dogen knows this too.
So he says, be careful that you hear the words "refrain from unwholesome action."
If you don't hear those words, you know it can't be the Buddha Dharma.
It must be some other crazy kind of Dharma, some kind of sensation-seeking, self-improving package that in the end is going to turn out bad.
It won't be the awakening that we truly seek.
When you hear these words "refrain from unwholesome action," they create a light in you.
All of a sudden, a light switch gets turned on.
The light was there before.
You were born with it, but it wasn't turned on.
Now it's switched on when you hear these words.
And you are going to realize that you want more than anything to vow to refrain from unwholesome action.
With that heart-turning word, you will embark on a very different path in your life.
You will no longer be compelled by worrying about how you are doing.
Are you rich or poor?
Is your status high or low?
Are you happy or unhappy?
That won't even matter to you anymore.
Are you successful or unsuccessful?
Are you helping anybody or not helping anybody?
All of these things will not matter to you anymore.
You will see in that light that all of that stuff is just suffering.
All of that stuff is beside the point.
And you will want only and simply to vow over and over again to refrain from unwholesome action, to make that vow the center of your life.
To refrain from unwholesome action, to do wholesome action, and to purify your mind.
And you will trust that when you devote yourself to practicing like that, fully and unreservedly committing yourself to it, everything is going to be okay.
Always.
Even when it's not.
Even when disasters happen.
And it is 100% guaranteed that disasters will happen.
It's still okay.
Because you will understand that your life is time.
Your life is all-inclusive.
Everything that you need is always going to be here, right in the middle of your life, regardless of the conditions.
He writes:
*When you refrain from unwholesome action, the power of practice is immediately actualized.
And it is actualized on the scale of the entire earth, the entire universe, all time, and all dharmas.*
That's the scale of "refrain from."
My brother somehow figured out how to share Kindle books.
There's a hack, somehow you can do that.
So he sends me Kindle books he likes, and he sent me a book about time, written by a physicist, but a good writer that you can understand, at least I could understand more or less.
And pretty much it says just that.
Pretty much.
We are all, every one of us, operating at the sacred, literal, exact center of the universe.
The place where the universe originated is literally where you are sitting.
Physics equations tell you that.
So we know it's true.
The physicists are the ones, the last authority on everything, right?
Pretty much, right, Bill?
So it's true.
Science now corroborates something that Dogen already knew.
So please, all of us, let's take our lives seriously.
Like that.
Let's forget about the rest of it.
It'll take care of itself.
We will sit with our whole heart in this way.
We'll get up and we'll go forth and we'll practice precepts.
Life will unfold.
Thank you very much for listening to my talk this morning.
Please don't let it distract you.
I hope you'll forget about it as soon as I'm gone and you'll just resume your sitting with strength.
Thank you very much.
Thank you very much.
